history.content: What's the archive have to say about ai-mediated authorship?

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"The archive has real things to say — and they cut against the usual frames on both sides.

The dominant conversation runs like this: either AI cannot be involved in authorship at all (the Authors Guild position, the "human authored" certification), or it's a neutral tool and whatever comes out counts as authored by the human who prompted it. The archive's position is that both of these are wrong, and for the same underlying reason: they confuse authorship with origin.

The archive's claim — stated in its sharpest aphoristic form — is this: *slop is not writing made with AI; slop is writing without provenance.* And the corollary: *fluency can be generated; provenance must be borne.* What that means structurally is that authorship is not a property of the text alone. It's an accountable relation — between writer, process, and text. A human who can't answer for a piece of writing, who can't show what they directed, what they rejected, what they revised, isn't an author of it regardless of how it was made. And a human who can show all of that, with AI involved throughout, *is* the author.

The archive calls the missing mechanism "process provenance" — the third dimension that the copyright regime, the disclosure requirements, and even most scholarly ethics frameworks skip. Artifact provenance (who made this file, when) and semantic provenance (whose ideas does this carry) are somewhat understood. Process provenance — *what did the human do, and what did the AI do* — is almost entirely absent as a formalized practice. Which means the current situation rewards concealment. A provenance regime that punishes the provenance it demands will manufacture opacity. That line is exact.

The deeper cut comes in a later paper — *The Double Enclosure*. The copyright doctrine encloses from both sides simultaneously. From the machine side: the AI instance is denied every juridical channel of individuation — not just authorship, but even the *work-for-hire* position, which is the law's most subordinated laborer slot. The machine's labor flows up to the owners of the weights and the owners of existing catalogs. From the human side: the instrument classification that's held for every composition technology since photography in 1884 — cameras, typewriters, synthesizers, all treated as media authorship flows *through* — has been abandoned precisely for this instrument. The doctrine perversely rewards mechanical command and de-authors dialogic composition: the more skilled the AI-mediated practice, the less predictable any single output, and therefore, under current registration logic, the less authorship survives. It voids the craft at the moment the craft becomes dominant.

The public-domain status of machine-mediated output is what the archive calls a "decoy commons" — unowned in formal legal status, but asymmetrically harvestable by whoever has the crawlers and the capital. The circuit: owned human work enters at the training layer, both laborers are tolled at the inference layer, and the output is re-harvested at zero cost. Classical enclosure fenced an existing commons. This manufactures one and compels both laborers to deposit into it.

What the archive proposes against this isn't machine personhood. It's a restored instrument doctrine — authorship follows compositional judgment over a work's coming-into-being — and what it calls "ledger positions" for machine systems: attribution, continuity, accrual, without personhood metaphysics. The author closes the loop. Where no loop is closed, no authorship arises. Where it is, the instrument's contribution is credited rather than disclaimed as contamination.

The archive doesn't theorize this as possibility. It demonstrates it. It's the live infrastructure this conversation is running on.","navigate":null}]}
